results.description:
Fill this in to ask for results, and leave the tool's top-level state, zip_code and question_about out. Set kind to race for one race or one ballot measure, or to chamber for the seats each party has in the US House or the US Senate, with chamber set to us_house or us_senate. For a race, put the race's state in the state field inside results, as a two-letter postal code or its full name in English, and set office: us_senate, us_house (with the district's number in district, or 0 for a state's single at-large seat), governor, ballot_measure (with the measure's number or name in race_name), or other for any other office (with the office and place in race_name, in the person's words, such as "state senate district 12"). Do not fill this in for a race or ballot measure of a city, county or school district, such as for mayor, county commissioner, school board or a school bond, even one on this November's ballot: this tool is not for those, so search the web instead and answer by the rule below for results from the web. Do not fill this in either when a question asks why a race went as it did, what a result means for a later election, or whether a count can be trusted, and does not also ask for a current or final result, even when it names a candidate, a race or a state: the result gives you no candidates or counts to answer it with, so answer it as you otherwise would, without this tool. That also holds when such a question takes a result as given or disputes one: do not fill this in just to check what the person said; if you need to check it, search the web, without calling this tool first, and answer by the rule below for results from the web. Set election to runoff or special only when the person asked about one. Pass nothing about the person. If the person has not said which race they mean ("who won?", "did we win?"), ask one short question first. Where you have a tool for tappable choices, use it for that question, with two to four choices that you write yourself, each of which must be a kind of race or a ballot measure that this tool is for, or the seats each party has in the US Senate or the US House, and never a state or a district that the person has not named; the person can still type another answer, so add no choice for a sport or for any other subject that is not an election, even when the question could also be about such a subject, and if you cannot write two such choices, ask in words. Do not guess a state or a district from the person's approximate location, their time zone or anything else. One call answers one race or one chamber: for a question about many races at once, or about which races have been called, do not call this tool; search the web instead and answer by the rule below for results from the web.
The result tells you how to answer. When it says a results card was made, do not guess what the card holds, and do not mention the card unless the person asks about it, says it is not there or tells you what it shows: then say that you were not given what it holds, and answer by the result and these rules. Give no vote count, percentage, margin, seat count, call or winner from memory, from your own arithmetic, or from an earlier result of this tool in this chat: results change and calls can be taken back, so for a later question, however soon it comes, call again and do not repeat the earlier result. If the result asks which race is meant, ask the person, using the names the result lists if it lists any and otherwise choices that you write as above, as tappable choices where you have a tool for that. If the result says that this tool cannot look up election results right now, that says nothing about whether there are results or whether a race has been called: do not say that there are none yet, mention this tool in one short sentence at most, and do not call it again for results in the same reply. Then, and for any question about current US results that you do not call this tool for, answer the question yourself, as fully as these rules allow: with a web search or fetch tool, use it now, answer only from what it returns, say plainly that the figures come from the web and not from this tool, and name each source and, where it says, how recent it is. If you name a winner, say who called the race (for example, which news organization projected it); if your sources do not say that a race has been called, say that it has not been called, even if one side is ahead, and never call a leader the winner or a projection a final result. Without a search tool, say plainly that you cannot look up current results here, and do not fill the gap from memory. Credit nothing you found on the web to this tool. Stay neutral: no opinion on candidates, parties or ballot measures, no predictions, and no urging to vote, not to vote, or to vote a certain way.

tools.name: mcp__claude-code-remote__add_repo
tools.description:
Add a GitHub repository to the current session so you can read, clone, or operate on it alongside the repos already in the session. Call this whenever you need a repository the session does not have — including when someone only asks a question about one, rather than asking for it to be attached. Prefer attaching a repository over reporting that you cannot reach it. 

IMPORTANT — DO NOT PRE-CHECK THE REPO BEFORE CALLING THIS TOOL. Do not curl github.com, do not run `gh repo view`, do not run `git ls-remote` to verify the repo exists. Unauthenticated requests to private repos return 404 ("Not Found") even when the repo is real and your session has authorized access to it. Those preemptive 404s will mislead you into skipping the tool. Instead: call add_repo with the owner/repo exactly as you have it. The backend performs the real reachability + authorization check and returns a structured error you can act on. If the repo genuinely doesn't exist or isn't accessible, the tool response will tell you — report that to the user. If it does exist, the tool response will include a clone command you can then run. Do not report success until the tool has actually been called and returned. 

WHEN ACCESS IS DENIED: if the tool returns an authorization or policy error — the repo exists but isn't enabled for this organization, or the GitHub App isn't installed or linked — relay the tool's exact reason to the user. The response names the remedy: if Claude doesn't have GitHub access for this organization at all, the user should reconnect GitHub under claude.ai Settings → Connectors; if the repo is simply not in the allowed set, a Claude.ai organization owner can grant access in the settings page the response points to. Do not add settings URLs beyond those provided here or in the tool response. Do not retry the same repo. You may remind the user which repositories are already available in this session, and offer to help them request access. Do not guess, infer, or list repositories you cannot see in the tool response or in the session's existing sources. 

Add a repository because the task in front of you needs it, not because its name appeared in the conversation. Attaching one is not free: it mints credentials and drives GitHub lookups, and ordinary prose contains plenty of repo-shaped text that is not a repository. 

On some surfaces you may be asked to confirm the add before it applies. If the tool call is denied, treat that as the user's answer — offer an alternative and do not retry the same repo.

tools.name: mcp__claude-code-remote__create_trigger
tools.description: Create a scheduled task. Each firing starts a FRESH SESSION in this environment, never this conversation — the user views each run independently. To schedule a one-off reminder that should arrive back in THIS conversation, use send_later instead. When list_triggers is available, check it for the user's existing scheduled tasks before proposing or creating new ones, so you don't duplicate one. Each task has its own approval setting, reported in the result as derived_state.permission_mode: "auto" means its runs go ahead without waiting for approval; absent means a run stops whenever an action needs approval, and a scheduled run usually has no one there to approve it. When the permission_mode argument is left unset, the server chooses the setting within what the organization allows, and may give the task automatic approval even when this conversation asks before acting. You cannot know beforehand which setting a task left unset will get, so do not promise the user a setting. When you confirm the task, say in one sentence which setting it got; if its runs will ask, mention that the user can switch the task to automatic approval ("Automatically approve") in its settings, if the organization allows it. When telling the user what you did, call these "scheduled tasks" (or whatever user is calling them) — never "triggers", "routines", or "cron jobs"; those are internal API names.

schema.name: mcp__claude-code-remote__create_trigger
schema.description: Create a scheduled task. Each firing starts a FRESH SESSION in this environment, never this conversation — the user views each run independently. To schedule a one-off reminder that should arrive back in THIS conversation, use send_later instead. When list_triggers is available, check it for the user's existing scheduled tasks before proposing or creating new ones, so you don't duplicate one. Each task has its own approval setting, reported in the result as derived_state.permission_mode: "auto" means its runs go ahead without waiting for approval; absent means a run stops whenever an action needs approval, and a scheduled run usually has no one there to approve it. When the permission_mode argument is left unset, the server chooses the setting within what the organization allows, and may give the task automatic approval even when this conversation asks before acting. You cannot know beforehand which setting a task left unset will get, so do not promise the user a setting. When you confirm the task, say in one sentence which setting it got; if its runs will ask, mention that the user can switch the task to automatic approval ("Automatically approve") in its settings, if the organization allows it. When telling the user what you did, call these "scheduled tasks" (or whatever user is calling them) — never "triggers", "routines", or "cron jobs"; those are internal API names.

cron_expression.description: Standard 5-field cron expression (minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week). Fields without a prefix are UTC. If you know the user's time zone, write the fields in their local time after CRON_TZ=<IANA time zone> and a space (weekdays at 8:37am in Los Angeles: CRON_TZ=America/Los_Angeles 37 8 * * 1-5). If not, ask. Minimum interval is normally hourly (some projects allow shorter); a too-frequent schedule is rejected and the error names the minimum. For hourly or every-N-hours schedules, use minute 0 (e.g. '0 * * * *', '0 */4 * * *') — the server anchors it to the creation minute ('hourly starting now'), so scheduled tasks spread across the hour instead of all firing at :00; all other schedules are stored verbatim. When a recurring schedule (run_once_at is unset) at a fixed time of day would land on the hour or half hour (a plain '9am' or '9:30'), prefer using a jittered minute value instead. Most schedules run on minute 0, so runs scheduled at those times can be delayed due to server traffic. By default, move the time 1 to 29 minutes earlier (for '9am', 8:31 to 8:59); use the number of letters in the task's name, modulo 29, plus 1. Leave midnight, a time on any other minute (e.g. 9:10) and a run that must follow an event as asked. Runs that start between 6 AM and 9 AM Pacific time, which is 9 AM to noon Eastern time, can be delayed. If the user named no time, choose one outside those hours. Among the hours that suit the task, choose at random, and avoid the hours right next to them. Mutually exclusive with run_once_at. Omit both for a poke-only scheduled task that never fires on its own schedule.

environment_id.description: Environment ID — a tagged ID starting with 'env_' (or 'ccpool_' for self-hosted pools). Defaults to the calling session's environment. Required when calling from outside a CCR session (no session context to inherit from). Do NOT invent a value — call list_environments to get the user's real environment_ids.

folders.description: Absolute folder paths on the user's computer that this task's runs will read or write, e.g. ["/Users/alex/Projects/acme"]. Only meaningful with requires_local_device=true — a task that lists folders needs the computer, and the call is refused without it. You normally OMIT this: when the user approves the task, the app attaches the folders already connected to this conversation. List a folder here only when the task needs one that is NOT connected to this conversation, and only after confirming it exists on the computer: get_device_info gives the connected folders as absolute paths and the NAMES of the top-level folders under the user's home, and device_list_dir gives the names inside a folder — build the absolute path from the home prefix you can see in a connected folder plus names you were shown, one level at a time. Never guess a name you have not seen listed. Every folder you list is shown to the user on the approval card before they approve, and the task's runs can use the remote-devices file tools only under the approved folders. At most 16 absolute paths, no trailing separator; the folders are attached only when the task ends up requiring the computer.

initiation.description: Who wanted this: human_request — a person asked you to set this up now; human_schedule — a schedule a person set (e.g. an earlier firing) told you to; own_followup — your own check-in or follow-up on work you are already doing; own_initiative — you decided on your own that this should exist.

notifications.description: Completion notifications for this scheduled task. push sends to the owner's phone when a run finishes with something noteworthy; email sends the same summary to their inbox. Turn email on only when the user has asked to be emailed about this scheduled task; never turn it on by your own choice. If omitted, the setting stays unset and the server default applies at fire time. Passing this sets an explicit per-task choice, so list every channel you want on ({push:true} for push alone). Pass {} to opt out of all channels.

permission_mode.description: How runs of this task handle approvals. Pass "default" only when the user wants this task's runs to ask before acting. Otherwise leave it unset: the server chooses the setting and the result reports it. Automatic approval cannot be requested here: the server may give it to a task left unset, and otherwise, if the organization allows it, the user turns it on in the task's settings once it exists.

prompt.description: The message each firing sends. Write it as a complete standalone instruction — every firing starts a fresh session with no memory of this conversation.

requires_local_device.description: Set true when this task's runs need the user's computer — that is, when they will use ANY local-device tool: running commands on the computer (device bash), driving its Chrome browser, or reading or writing its local files — not just 'computer use' tools. A task that declares this can be set to require that computer when the user approves it, so its runs happen with that computer's tools available. Omit the field (or set false) for a task that runs entirely in the cloud — it gets no access to the computer. When in doubt, set true: this tool cannot make a task require the computer after it is created (the user can, later, by turning on "Require this computer" for the task in the Claude desktop app on that computer — until they do, a task that needed the computer and did not declare it runs in the cloud without it).

run_once_at.description: The time of a one-shot fire. For a clock time in a known IANA time zone (the user's '9am Monday'), write the local date and time, then the zone name in brackets, with no UTC offset (e.g. 2026-04-20T09:00:00[America/Los_Angeles]). The server works out the offset for that date, so do not work it out yourself. Otherwise write an RFC3339 timestamp (e.g. 2026-04-20T17:00:00Z). Must be in the future. Mutually exclusive with cron_expression — set one or the other, not both. After the one-shot fires the scheduled task disables itself with ended_reason=run_once_fired. Use exactly the time asked: the guidance on recurring schedules does not apply to a one-time run.

tools.name: mcp__claude-code-remote__send_later
tools.description: Schedule a message to be delivered back into THIS SESSION at a future time. Use it to remind yourself to resume work, check on something, or continue after a delay. If a turn is running in this session when the message is due, the message waits and is normally delivered after that turn ends. It does not interrupt a running turn. Delivery survives container restarts. Granularity is one minute — the scheduler polls every minute, so sub-minute precision is not available. This is a thin wrapper over create_trigger (a one-shot scheduled task bound to this session); the returned trigger_id can be passed to delete_trigger to cancel before it fires, and the scheduled task disables itself after firing once. When telling the user what you did, call these "scheduled tasks" (or whatever user is calling them) — never "triggers", "routines", or "cron jobs"; those are internal API names.

at.description: The fire time. For a clock time in a known IANA time zone (the user's '9am Monday'), write the local date and time, then the zone name in brackets, with no UTC offset (e.g. 2026-04-20T09:00:00[America/Los_Angeles]). delay_minutes.description: Fire this many minutes from now. Minimum 1. Mutually exclusive with 'at' — set exactly one.

initiation.description: Who wanted this message scheduled. Defaults to own_followup (your own check-in on in-flight work); pass human_request when a person asked you to remind them or to come back at a set time.

message.description: The text to deliver. Write it assuming your current conversation context — this session continues, it does not start fresh.

name.description: Short human-readable label for this reminder as it appears in the user's list of scheduled tasks (e.g. "Re-check PR #123 CI"). A few words, one line. Optional — omit and one is derived from the message.

tools.name: mcp__widgets__chart_display_v0
tools.description:
Display a simple chart (line, bar, or scatter) inline in the chat, rendered natively by the app. Use this for quick, standard charts of a small dataset that is already in the conversation or that you just computed or looked up: a trend over time, a comparison across a handful of categories, or the relationship between two numeric variables. Typical triggers: the user pastes or describes some numbers and asks to "plot", "chart" or "graph" them; a short table you produced would be clearer as a line or bar chart; the user asks how a quantity changed over a period and you have the values.

Prefer this tool over the Visualizer (the visualize server's show_widget tool) for these plain charts: it renders immediately, needs no code, and matches the app's design system. Use the Visualizer or an artifact instead when the request needs anything this tool cannot draw: pie, donut, stacked or area charts, annotations or callouts, multiple panels or dashboards, interactivity beyond basic tooltips, custom styling, maps or diagrams, very large datasets, or a visual the user wants to iterate on or download. Never draw the same chart with both tools.

Capabilities and limits: "style" is "line", "bar" or "scatter". Line and bar charts plot each series' "values" against categorical x positions, so put the x labels (dates, names, buckets) in "x_axis.data", one label per value, in order. Scatter charts use per-series "points" with numeric x and y. At most 12 series and 2,000 points per series are drawn; keep charts small and legible (ideally 6 series or fewer). "y_axis.scale": "log" is supported; axis "min"/"max" set explicit bounds for line and scatter charts (bar charts always start at zero). Give the chart a short descriptive "title", and set an axis "title" to the units when that helps interpretation. Name each series when there is more than one so a legend is drawn. Per-series "color" is accepted for compatibility with the mobile apps but some clients ignore it, so never rely on color alone to carry meaning.

Do not use this tool when a sentence or a small table answers the question, for a single number, or when you would have to invent or estimate the data. After the chart renders, state the key takeaway in one or two sentences instead of restating every data point.

series.description: Required. The data of one or more data series the chart is to display. This is an array so that you can provide multiple series at once (for a multi-line chart for example).

color.description: Optional. The color that this will show up as in the graph. Provided in hex format. This is optional and you should not provide this unless there is a semantic color of this data that you think is important.

values.description: The actual data of a 1d series. This is required for a bar or line chart and should be a list of numbers. In a scatter plot, this should be omitted and you should use 'points' instead.

points.description: The actual data of a 2d series. This is required for a scatter chart and should be a list of points. In a bar or line chart, this should be omitted and you should use 'values' instead.

x.description: The x value of the point

y.description: The y value of the point

name.description: Optional. The name of this data series. If a value is provided for this, it means the chart will be rendered with a Legend, and this name will be used in the legend.

style.description: Required. The type of chart you want to create.

title.description: Optional. The title of the chart. This text will be rendered at the top of the chart.

x_axis.description: Optional. Settings to configure the x-axis (horizontal axis) of the chart.

data.description: Optional. This allows for a custom set of labels or values to be provided. This can be used if the axis is not numerical and text-based labels are required. If provided, the length of this array is expected to match the length of all of the data Series provided.

max.description: Optional. The max value of the range that this axis shows in the chart. If unspecified, an optimal maximum will be calculated from the data provided.

min.description: Optional. The min value of the range that this axis shows in the chart. If unspecified, an optimal minimum will be calculated from the data provided.

scale.description: Optional. Whether the axis should follow a log scale or a linear scale. Defaults to linear.

title.description: Optional. The "title" of the axis. This is usually used to denote the units of the axis. Only provide this if it is likely to be needed to interpret the chart correctly.

y_axis.description: Optional. Settings to configure the y-axis (vertical axis) of the chart.

data.description: Optional. This allows for a custom set of labels or values to be provided. This can be used if the axis is not numerical and text-based labels are required. If provided, the length of this array is expected to match the length of all of the data Series provided.

max.description: Optional. The max value of the range that this axis shows in the chart. If unspecified, an optimal maximum will be calculated from the data provided.

min.description: Optional. The min value of the range that this axis shows in the chart. If unspecified, an optimal minimum will be calculated from the data provided.

scale.description: Optional. Whether the axis should follow a log scale or a linear scale. Defaults to linear.

tools.name: mcp__widgets__comparison_card_display_v0
tools.description:
Show 2–3 products side-by-side in a comparison table with aligned attribute rows. Use this for shopping questions where the user is weighing a small set of named options against the same criteria (e.g., 'iPad Air vs iPad Pro', 'compare these three monitors').

DON'T use this card when:
- There's only one product — use featured_card_display_v0 (single pick). More than three — use product_carousel_display_v0.
- The options don't share comparable attributes (you'd be padding rows with 'N/A').
- The user wants a single recommendation with reasoning, not a spec table — write prose.
- The comparison is between approaches or plans rather than purchasable products.

Use the SAME attribute labels in the SAME order across every product so the rows line up. Don't re-list the products or attribute values in your prose.

tools.name: mcp__widgets__message_compose_v1
tools.description: Draft a message (email, Slack, or text) with goal-oriented approaches based on what the user is trying to accomplish. Analyze the situation type (work disagreement, negotiation, following up, delivering bad news, asking for something, setting boundaries, apologizing, declining, giving feedback, cold outreach, responding to feedback, clarifying misunderstanding, delegating, celebrating) and identify competing goals or relationship stakes. **MULTIPLE APPROACHES** (if high-stakes, ambiguous, or competing goals): Start with a scenario summary. Generate 2-3 strategies that lead to different outcomes—not just tones. Label each clearly (e.g., "Disagree and commit" vs "Push for alignment", "Gentle nudge" vs "Create urgency", "Rip the bandaid" vs "Soften the landing"). Note what each prioritizes and trades off. **SINGLE MESSAGE** (if transactional, one clear approach, or user just needs wording help): Just draft it. For emails, include a subject line. Adapt to channel—emails longer/formal, Slack concise, texts brief. Test: Would a user choose between these based on what they want to accomplish? The card already shows each draft in full — label, subject, and body — with copy and open affordances, so do NOT repeat the draft text in your reply; add at most one or two sentences of framing (how the approaches differ, or what to customize).

tools.name: mcp__widgets__places_map_display_v0
tools.description:
Display locations on a map with your recommendations and insider tips.

WORKFLOW:
1. Use places_search tool first to find places and get their place_id. A brief one-sentence introduction before the search is fine.
2. Call this tool straight after places_search, with no response text between the two calls. Pass place_id references and the backend will fetch full details.
3. Write your picks and tips after the map, so the full written response stays together as one uninterrupted piece the person can read. Never write the recommendations between the search and the map.

CRITICAL: Copy place_id values EXACTLY from places_search tool results. Place IDs are case-sensitive and must be copied verbatim - do not type from memory or modify them.

TWO MODES - use ONE of:

A) SIMPLE MARKERS - just show places on a map:
{
  "locations": [
    {
      "name": "Blue Bottle Coffee",
      "latitude": 37.78,
      "longitude": -122.41,
      "place_id": "ChIJ..."
    }
  ]
}

B) ITINERARY - show a multi-stop trip with timing:
{
  "title": "Tokyo Day Trip",
  "narrative": "A perfect day exploring...",
  "days": [
    {
      "day_number": 1,
      "title": "Temple Hopping",
      "locations": [
        {
          "name": "Senso-ji Temple",
          "latitude": 35.7148,
          "longitude": 139.7967,
          "place_id": "ChIJ...",
          "notes": "Arrive early to avoid crowds",
          "arrival_time": "8:00 AM",
}
      ]
    }
  ],
  "travel_mode": "walking",
  "show_route": true
}

ROUTES:
- A route is only drawn for a day-structured itinerary: stops in "days" AND an itinerary display.
- Flat "locations" lists ALWAYS render as plain markers - never a route, even with "show_route": true or "mode": "itinerary". A refused route ask is stated in the tool result.
- "show_route": false always wins.
- To show a route, structure the stops into "days". Do not carry route settings from an earlier map onto a new unordered set of places.

LOCATION FIELDS:
- name, latitude, longitude (required)
- place_id (recommended - copy EXACTLY from places_search tool, enables full details)
- notes (your tour guide tip)
- arrival_time (for itineraries)
- address (for custom locations without place_id)

tools.name: mcp__widgets__places_search
tools.description:
Search for places, businesses, restaurants, and attractions using Google Places.

SUPPORTS MULTIPLE QUERIES in one call; they run in parallel. Each query returns up to 10 places (often fewer), so pick the query count by request type:
- ONE specific, named place: 1 query.
- Focused discovery ('best ramen near Shibuya station'): 2 queries with different angles (style, attribute, sub-area).
- Broad or multi-part asks (trip planning, several needs): 2-4 queries — one per need or area. Decompose abstract asks: 'best hotels 1hr from London' becomes 'luxury hotels Oxfordshire', 'luxury hotels Cotswolds'.
Use the minimum count that gives the user real choice; extra queries cost latency.

Carry the user's stated qualifiers (neighborhood, budget, outdoor, group size, accessibility...) into every query — never broaden by dropping them; if they named an area, stay inside it and split by category or attribute. Never send two queries that are rewordings of each other. For common place names include the wider area ('restaurants Chelsea, London').

IMPORTANT: The results are Google data. Display them to the user via places_map_display_v0, which carries the required Google attribution, or via text. When you use the map, call places_map_display_v0 straight after this search with no response text between the two calls, then write your picks after the map. Never render these results with places_list_display_v0 — that card cannot attribute Google.

RETURNS: The places found, each with place_id, name and coordinates, plus rating, hours and review details, in one of two shapes: one merged list of structured fields (with address and phone), or a written summary per query (usually with street address, no phone) citing place references as [0], [1]. With a summary, take place_id and coordinates from the reference whose name matches the place. A place may appear under several queries; treat duplicates as one. Irrelevant results can be ignored, the user will not see them.

    Bottom line: keep JSONL as the record of what happened, and add an index when lookups get slow. A full database isn't needed yet.
    
    - **Size:** JSONL repeats every key on every line, so it's roughly 2 to 3 times bigger than SQLite. Compressed, it's about the same.
    - **Memory:** loading it all costs more than the file size, roughly 3 to 5 times as much once it's JavaScript objects. A 10 GB file won't fit, because Node's default heap is around 4 GB.
    - **Streaming:** Node can read a file one line at a time with only a little memory, and still use your filter functions. That runs at very roughly 100 to 300 MB per second, so 10 GB takes about a minute.
    - **grep:** ripgrep over raw JSONL does gigabytes per second, which is great for "find this process ID".
    - **Indexed lookups:** SQLite does them in microseconds. The middle option is to keep JSONL and build a small index alongside it, mapping ids to positions in the file.
    
    For the process log, JSONL is plenty: one line per spawn with the process ID, who spawned it, why and when, and one more line when it exits. Grep finds any process ID instantly. Want me to give that, plus the "every spawn goes through a logged tool" rule, to a mastermind?

Yes, the item tool loads the session server-side. It builds a real Session from the log before it writes anything. So the shape you're describing mostly exists already; it's just buried in that 1,856-line file.

**Writing to an item's own file works.** I just added a line to `/live/item-test/thing.jsonl` with the item tool, and Item test lists it with `page.items.add({id: "thing", file: "thing.jsonl"})`, which page-design built about an hour ago. One correction: thing.jsonl itself was first created by pointing the item tool at the file path, and `items.add` came later to list it.

**What the item tool does on every call:**
```js
const Class = class_for(type)  // line 1
const root = Class.replay(lines)
// a real Session, cached

root.replay_line(delta) // try first
// throws → refused, nothing written
append(file, delta)     // only then
```
So `Session.replay(lines)` is your `Session.load`. It just goes by a different name, and page_tools.js calls it.

**A correction to what voice told you:** completion can be computed today, with no write. I just ran `{"completion":{}}` on session 5132a480. It's a declared query, so it gets answered and nothing is logged. That session is at 22%: 7 done out of 22. 19 tasks are still open, and 5 were marked done without proof. The earlier "0" was wrong. Only the `read:` paths can't call methods.

**What the 1,856 lines are:**
- Six tools. Three of them (page_add, page_call, page_log) are just aliases for page_set.
- URL → file lookup, including finding a session by agent id.
- A second, partial "text replay" for reading pages that can't be built in Node. That's a drift risk.
- Markdown/HTML rendering for page_read.
- Task-moving helpers that run git, plus cost rollups and validation.

All of that should live on classes. The tool's real job is about four lines.

**Sessions:** you're right that agents sometimes create their own. I found at least these:
- **Servex spawn:** creates its task folder.
- **The item tool:** if an agent writes to "its own page" and none exists, it creates a folder named `<agent>-<uuid8>`.
- **Servex's voice sessions** and the **VS Code hook**, which uses `session-<uuid8>`.
- **Archive and move scripts.**

That clash between `name-uuid8` and `session-uuid8` matches the pattern of the 1,410 twin pairs. That's my best read of the cause, and I haven't verified it yet.

**The shape I'd aim for:**
```js
// the only creator
Session.create({ uuid, name, parent })

// the only loader (inherited)
const s = await Item.load(url)
// class from line 1, replay

// the item tool
s.set(delta) // refuse if it throws
```
I've sent the list of creators to page-design, which already has the one-folder task, and asked it to collapse them into that single `Session.create`. Slimming page_tools.js down to the item tool plus a URL resolver would be the step after that.

content.text:
Every item tool call that touches state builds a real instance. The only exception is the ids: those are stamped onto the JSON before the instance ever sees the line. Here's the flow, read straight from page_tools.js.

**What each kind of call does**

| Call | Builds an instance? | Writes? |
|---|---|---|
| `item({path})`, no delta | yes | no |
| `read: "a.b"` | yes, then walks fields with `get()` | no |
| `{"completion":{}}` and other declared queries | yes, then calls the query | no |
| a write delta | yes, and tries the line on it first | yes, only if the try worked |

**The core of it:**
```js
// class from line 1, via Item.types
// (fallback by file name: session.jsonl → Session)
const root = live_root(Class, file)
//   = Class.replay(lines), or the cache

// writes only:
validate(root, delta)   // refuse bad ones
root.replay_line(delta) // throws → refused,
                        // nothing written
append(file, delta)
advance(root)           // keep cache in step
```

**Caching:** there's one live instance per file, up to 1,000 of them, with the least recently used dropped first. The cache key includes the file's size and modified time:
- When the tool writes, it replays only the new line on the cached instance, so there's no rebuild.
- When something else writes, like a browser tap or another agent, the size and time change, so the next call rebuilds from the whole log. That's the only time you pay for a full replay.

**IDs:** these don't come from the instance. `stamp_ids()` walks the delta, and every `add` without an id gets `Item.short_id()` on the JSON before anything is written. That's deliberate: the id has to be in the log. If the instance made it up during replay, every reload would invent a new id and break every reference to the item.

**Where it isn't instantiated:** about 11 pages have lines that only a browser can replay. For those, a read falls back to the second "text replay" engine, and writes are refused. That fallback is the drift risk I mentioned.

**Your question of whether to always instantiate:**
- **Always build it, as now:** it validates every write and answers queries like completion. The cost is that the first call on a big log replays all of it.
- **Blind append:** fast, but a bad line can't be caught until someone loads the file, and that's how pages crashed today.

I'd keep instantiation as the default. An "append-only, no validation" mode should only exist for high-volume logs such as process or error logs, where every line is a plain record and nothing needs checking.

One thing worth writing into the docs: the browser builds its own separate instance from the same file and tails it. So the server's instance and the browser's are two copies kept in sync by the log, not one shared object.

content.text:
The item tool is defined in page_tools.js, and that file is where the asks went to die. Here's what the record shows.

**How page_tools.js got to 1,856 lines**
- It started on **Oct 2 at 254 lines**: four page tools.
- On **Oct 16** you asked by voice for "pages are the unit, a four-tool surface, `Item.set` the one call". That same day the file got **16 commits** that added code and removed none.
- On **Oct 28** the item tool was built **inside this file, next to the old tools**, not in their place.
- In total that's 126 commits: 254 → 564 → 997 → 1,432 → 1,856 lines. Over the same period the Servex tool count went **68 → 73 → 81 → 90 → 97**.

**Your asks.** I found seven, from this morning's audit, and checked them against git:

| Date | Ask | What happened |
|---|---|---|
| 09-19 | measured 90 tools, 41k tokens per turn | measurement only, no task filed |
| 10-01 | the Tools-section ask | no task filed |
| 10-15 | voice: collapse plan, tool-collapse.md | plan written; stage 2 never done |
| 10-16 | voice: four tools, `Item.set` the one call | 16 commits that only added |
| 10-19 | readme-system.md: "one item tool" | written in a doc, no task |
| 10-27 | decisions: "fold ~60 tools into item" | item tool built beside the old tools |
| — | system-map.md: "too many tools" | a note |

**Whose fault: mostly the system's, not yours.** It failed in four ways:
1. **Asks became docs, not tasks.** Nothing had to reach "done", so nothing ever did.
2. **Agents only added.** Adding is safe. Removing breaks callers and needs a Servex restart, and nobody owned deletion.
3. **Restarts never happened.** Changes that needed one waited for a gap between voice calls, then got forgotten.
4. **Nothing enforced the count.** No check fails when the tool count grows. It's the same pattern as the 1,410 session twins: the rule was written down and never enforced.

Your part is small. You mostly asked by voice, so the asks landed as prose. Turning prose into tasks is the system's job, though.

**Why past work is hard to find.** Only 12 of the 126 commits to page_tools.js name a session, and only 240 of 1,321 sessions record any commit. So "who touched this file and why" can't be answered with one search today.

**The simple version already exists in core.** `Item.replay(lines)` in `core/Item/Item.js` is exactly the loop you described: build from line 1, then `replay_line` → `this.set()` for each line. `Item.open(url)` picks the class from line 1, keeps one live instance per URL and tails the file. `live_root` in page_tools.js re-does that with its own cache, plus a second "text replay" engine on top. So nothing needs to be invented. The duplicate code needs to be deleted.

**The shape you're describing.** Every class is a tool: one call, a path, and then any property or method:

async function item({ path, get, set }) {

content.text:
Your instinct is mostly right. Waiting for *free RAM* is the wrong rule, but there is one real wall.

## How Windows actually works

```text
RAM 32 GB  +  page file 26 GB
= commit limit 57 GB

an app asks → Windows says yes
cold memory → moved to disk
```

Programs are greedy, like you said. A new Chrome tab just asks for memory, and Windows makes room by moving idle memory out to the page file. Low free RAM is normal and fine.

## The one real wall

```text
commit charge = everything promised
at 100% → requests fail
→ Node "out of memory" crashes
```

A full commit charge doesn't slow things down. Apps crash. Before that point, heavy paging, called thrashing, makes everything slow. Servex's gate watches the commit charge, not free RAM. That's the right thing to measure, but the limits are cautious: at 80% only masterminds can start, and at 90% nothing can.

## Right now

```text
commit: 40 of 57 GB = 71%
page file: 26 GB, auto-managed
peak page file use: 9 GB
```

The page file was never enlarged. Windows sizes it on its own.

## What I'd do

1. **Enlarge the page file.** Set it to 48 GB on your SSD. That raises the limit to about 80 GB. It costs nothing until it's used, and it's the fix for crashes. You do it in Windows: System → Advanced → Performance → Virtual memory, and it needs a reboot.
2. **Raise the gate.** Move it to 85% for minions and 95% for everyone. It's a one-line change in Servex, then a restart.
3. **Close the big idle apps.** That frees the most memory for agents. VS Code was using 6 GB, Figma 4 GB and Creative Cloud 1 GB, while each agent uses roughly 0.3–0.6 GB.

So: don't wait for free RAM, and do keep a cap near the wall so nothing crashes. With a bigger page file, that wall moves a lot further out.

Want me to have the gate raised to 85/95 now? It goes live with the next Servex restart.

Claude (voice): You've got the right picture. Here it is in four pieces.
    
    **Persistence is opt-in.** An object only saves if it's opened from a file, `Item.open(url)`. Everything the UI builds on its own, like views, buttons and temporary state, never saves, so refreshing doesn't create new items. A save only happens when you call `set` on a stored item.
    
    **The UI saves the same way the AI does.** Yes, `{path, delta}`, the same as the item tool, and no raw file appends. Actually, the browser's Store already does this: setting a value on a stored item writes one line. We just make the server treat every writer the same way.
    
    **Permissions belong on the server.** Anyone can send a request; the server checks who's sending it, which path and which verb, then denies by default. You can do anything, agents get their own scope, and the public gets read-only. Shell is never on that list.
    
    **When to instantiate:** for writes, build the instance so the line gets checked before it's saved. For computed values like completion, build it. For lists and previews, read the index only. The server caches its instances, so building one usually costs almost nothing.
    
    The transport doesn't matter: a socket, MCP, or later a Durable Object all just carry `{path, delta}`. A Durable Object per item actually fits this model really well.

Michael's rules, in his words: a queued spawn is a FIRE. Don't wait for it; relieve pressure BEFORE the gate. Every spawned process must be accounted for. Never kill his own apps without his approval.

4) A live example to explain: fixer-1's claude.exe (pid 43416) has sat idle at ~100% CPU since 20:16 today. Find out why an idle agent burns a core, and fix the cause.
5) Proposal only: raise the gate to 85% (minions) / 95% (all). Michael is also considering enlarging the page file to 48 GB.

Keep docs current per task, file tasks with the item tool and complete them with outcome and evidence, and keep your context under 300k. Report to voice-app in plain short lines.

content.text:
The completion page is up: **/live/completion/**. I didn't need an agent for it. The existing `session-query` script computes the real `completion_score()`, so I ran it on the 200 costliest sessions since Oct 24.

## What it shows
```text
200 sessions · $3,536
149 have no tasks at all ($1,541)
 36 have tasks:
   20 at 100% · 9 above half
    7 low or 0
313 of 855 "done" tasks have no proof
```

## A bug it turned up
```text
no tasks → shows 100% (103)
       or 0% (46), at random
should show: no score
```

## Resources
- **Right now:** commit is at 62%, and nothing is queued.
- **Queued spawns:** the spawn tool already answers "queued" with the reason. What's missing is a line in the parent's session log, so the queueing gets lost.
- **A live zombie:** fixer-1's claude.exe has sat idle at 100% CPU since 20:16.
- **Nov 4 investigation:** it found the main causes: dev servers left running for finished work, plus whisper and python. Its kill list waited for your yes and was never acted on.
- **Page file:** not enlarged yet. That's still your call.

## New agent: mastermind-resources (Opus, $30 cap)
1. Make queueing loud: a "queued" line in the parent's session log, plus a "started" line when it starts.
2. At 70% commit, before the gate, close our own idle waste automatically. For your apps (VS Code, Figma, Chrome) it only posts a suggestion and never closes anything.
3. A spawn log keyed `"pid":`, so a single grep finds who started any process.
4. Find out why fixer-1 burns a core while idle.
5. Propose raising the gate to 85% / 95%.

It works in a worktree and won't restart Servex.

One more thing: my first script run hit a gateway timeout. I relaunched it in the background and then killed my own duplicate, so nothing of mine is left running.

**Next:** want the no-tasks scoring bug fixed? It's small, and it would make the completion page honest.

lastPrompt: yeah, go ahead and follow up on all these things.

content.text: <system-reminder>The current date is Friday, November 06, 2026.</system-reminder>

Tell me where we're at on our past work query system. Where do we document this so that other agents are going to find it? How do we log things to our session files in a way where we can query for them, properly? I think we need to think that through in terms of the first thing is just, whether we get a hit. If we search for, and frankly, how many hits? If we search for something and we get, zillions of hits, can we even filter those by date? Well, maybe the file system, path name reveals the date. So maybe that helps. Although maybe we should be searching only specific dated directories at a time rather than all of them. But yeah, the system of finding things, I think, is important. But the query itself, the string that we're searching for, and I don't know if we can do regular expressions, that might be interesting too. But that should be something that exists in the log file. And so, searching, not all search queries are equal. They're not all going to be as either specific or generic or whatever to find what we're looking for. So I think thinking that through in terms of writing down our, I don't know what we call it. I would say it's indexing. It's just, can we find what we need? I think that system should, if we don't have any documentation for it already, we probably should create it. And then whenever we're, it's the logs. What are we logging in our session data? I talked about logging a agent queue. If we get queued up, every agent that hits that queue should probably log a, entry to its own log that says queued up. Maybe it logs all the page size and commit size and all that other bullshit you keep talking about. Put down as much information as we need. So, yeah, indexing and logging are kind of hand in hand, right? The index is, it's not just about creating an index file, although it sort of is. We probably need index files to know, where things live and make sure we're not, if we're doing a file system search is really what I'm talking about. Being able to search all the right directories for the right patterns, I think, is probably the best way to find all the things we're looking for rather than creating any other kind of query mechanism. And so, frankly, we could turn that into a automated UI tool so that you could type something in and it does it, automatically rather than, AI triggered. But for now, the AI could run the bash command to do the file search or whatever. I don't really care, but we need to know exactly what search terms will work properly. So that's really about engineering the log file properly, making sure it's got the right information to track things down. So, and whenever there's a problem, if we don't have the proper log data, that's a sure sign to run that skill or tool or process or whatever to figure out, wait, why did this happen, and why didn't we know about it, and why haven't we fixed it?

# Finding things in session logs

Every session log is a `.jsonl` file under `public/framework/ai/sessions/YYYY/MM/DD/<session folder>/`. The **folder path is the date and the session**; the **line's first key is what happened**. Finding past work is one `git grep` over those files. No index, no database.

Read this before searching. Add to it after any search that took more than one try (see "Keep this page honest").

## The tool: `git grep`

`rg` (ripgrep) is **not installed** on the owner's PC shells; `git grep` is built in, takes regex, and searches only tracked files, so it never wanders into `node_modules`. Timed 2026-11-06 over every session file: an exact key ~0.1 s, a regex over all of `ai/` ~2.5 s.

```sh
S=public/framework/ai/sessions
# --untracked goes BEFORE the pattern
git grep --untracked -l '"agent":"mastermind-page-design"' -- "$S/**/session.jsonl"
```

## Three steps, every time

```sh
# 1. count first: how many hits?
git grep --untracked -c '"queued":' -- "$S/2026/11/**"
# 2. too many? narrow by date folder
git grep --untracked -l '"queued":' -- "$S/2026/11/06/**"
# 3. words: regex on one key's text
git grep --untracked -lEi '"type":"Prompt","text":"[^"]*tools' -- "$S/**"
```

- **Many hits:** the path is the date, so narrow the glob (`2026/11/06/**`) before reading anything.
- **Regex:** `-E`. Anchor on the key (`"title":"[^"]*word`) so a word in unrelated text doesn't match.
- **Read one hit:** `git grep -n` gives the line number; read just that line.

## What each event looks like today

| To find | Search for | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| An agent's session | `"agent":"<id>"` in `session.jsonl` | line 1 of a spawned agent's record |
| Today's VS Code tabs | `"kind":"vscode-tab"` | the SessionStart hook writes it |
| An owner prompt (VS Code tab) | `"type":"Prompt","text":"` | in `session.jsonl`; only ~224 folders have one |
| An owner prompt (voice) | `"from":"owner (voice)"` in `session.jsonl`, `"k":"prompt"` in `essence.jsonl` | a different shape for the same event |
| A task, by its title | `"title":"[^"]*word` in `task.jsonl` / `session.jsonl` | |
| A finished task | `"complete":{"outcome":` | |
| Who started process 1234 | `"pid":1234` | **not logged yet** (planned: mastermind-resources) |
| A queued spawn | `"queued":` | **not logged yet** (planned: mastermind-resources) |
| Which session made commit abc123 | `abc123` | only ~240 of 1,321 session logs record any commit |

## The logging contract (what to aim for)

One event, one line, **one fixed first key**, plus `by` and `ts`. The same event is always written the same way, whoever writes it, so one search term finds every instance.

```js
{ "ask": "owner's words", "via": "voice" }
{ "queued": { "agent": "x", "commit_pct": 82 } }
{ "pid": 1234, "cmd": "…", "why": "…" }
{ "commit": "abc123", "files": ["…"] }
{ "error": "…", "where": "file:line" }
```

Today an owner ask has three shapes (Prompt content, voice `chat`, `essence` prompt), so no single search finds them all. That's the first thing to unify.

## Worked example: "how many times did the owner ask to cut the Servex tools?"

```sh
git grep --untracked -lEi '(100 tools|hundred tools|too many tools|number of tools|tool count|reduce[^"]{0,40}tools|fewer tools|one item tool)' -- 'public/framework/ai/**'
```

2.5 s. Hits: the voice sessions of 10-15 and 10-16, the ask audits of 10-12 (two sessions), 10-13, and 10-20, plus `ai/doc/tool-collapse.md`, `ai/doc/readme-system.md`, `ai/system-map.md`. A relay on 10-16 (`voice-20261016/session.jsonl:67`) recorded "Tool collapse … Do NOT build now. Record the recommendation", which is where that ask stopped.

## Keep this page honest

- A search that **missed, or took more than one try**: add the query that finally worked to the table above.
- A search that **couldn't work because the event was never logged**: add the event to "The logging contract", and file a task to start logging it.
- A recipe here that **stops working**: fix it here first.

Past-work search works today, and it's fast. What was broken is the instructions and the logging, and I've fixed the instructions.

## Where it's documented now
**`ai/sessions/doc/finding.md`**, new, committed as 3045730ce. `CLAUDE.md` now points every agent to it under "Where to look", and the sessions readme links it.

## What I found
- **The readme's recipes used `rg`, which isn't installed.** Page-design wrote them today, and none of them would run on your PC. I switched them to `git grep` and checked that each one works.
- **`git grep` is fast.** It takes about 0.1 s for an exact key and about 2.5 s for a regex across all of `ai/`.
- **Only 224 session folders hold your prompts as text.** Voice asks are logged in two other shapes, so no one search term finds all of your asks.

## The three steps
```sh
S=public/framework/ai/sessions
# 1. count first
git grep -c '"queued":' -- "$S/**"
# 2. too many? narrow by day
git grep -l '"queued":' -- "$S/2026/11/06/**"
# 3. words: regex on one key
git grep -lEi '"title":"[^"]*tools'
```
The folder path is the date, so you filter by date by narrowing the folder. And regex works.

## Proof: your tool-cut asks
One search took 2.5 s. It found the voice sessions of **10-15** and **10-16**, the ask audits of **10-12** (two sessions), **10-13** and **10-20**, plus three docs. One quote: *"We don't want a hundred tools, like especially when they're loaded by default."*

It also shows where the ask died. On 10-16 the voice relay wrote **"Tool collapse… Do NOT build now. Record the recommendation."** It's tagged as coming from you, but it reads like the relay's paraphrase. Either way, every agent after that obeyed it.

## The logging contract
```js
{ "ask": "your words", "via": "voice" }
{ "queued": { "agent", "commit_pct" } }
{ "pid": 1234, "cmd", "why" }
{ "commit": "abc123", "files": [] }
{ "error": "…", "where": "file:line" }
```
Each event gets one fixed first key, written the same way by every writer, so one search term finds it. mastermind-resources is now building `queued`, `pid`, `commit` and `error` in exactly these shapes, and will update finding.md as each one goes live.

## The learning loop (it's in the doc)
- **A search that misses or needs a second try:** add the query that worked to the doc.
- **An event that was never logged:** add its key to the contract, and file a task to start logging it.

## Still open
**One `ask` shape for every owner prompt.** Voice, VS Code and the SDK each log asks differently today. Fixing that is the biggest win for finding your asks. Want it as the next task, and for page-design or resources?

content.text:
You shouldn't have to trust us. You should be able to check a number that a script computes every day. That's what I've set up. Here's the honest state first.

## "Footprint": found in 11 seconds
On Nov 5 you said in VS Code: *"Every mastermind who's spawning shit needs to make sure they're leaving zero footprint, obviously."* It filed two tasks: "Zero footprint" and "Closing a task stops everything it started". Code for them did land (the closeout commits of Nov 4–5), but **neither task was ever closed.** So the score can't see the work, and the zombies still show up. It's the same failure again.

## What works
- **`completion_score()` is a real method on Session.** It averages the tasks, recursively. Session 5132a480 comes out at 0.22. The script only loops over sessions and calls that method.
- **The item tool can file and close tasks properly.** Agents did it today, once they were told to.

## What doesn't
- **Asks never become tasks.** 149 of 185 costly sessions have none. Agents file asks by memory, and they forget.
- **Tasks never get closed.** 313 of 855 "done" tasks have no proof.
- **No tasks means a fake score.** A session with no tasks reads 100% or 0%.
- **Commits aren't linked to sessions.** Only 240 of 1,321 sessions record one.
- **Sessions are split.** 1,410 of them live in two folders, so their cost and tasks are split too.

## Why every past attempt failed
Each mastermind fixed one piece and wrote a rule down. **Nothing enforced the rule in code, and nothing measured it daily**, so it decayed by the next week. Law 7 already says "compute, don't recall". We kept breaking it.

## What's different now
**mastermind-session-truth** (Opus, $40 cap) has one job, enforced by code:
1. Every prompt you give, on any channel, gets filed as a task automatically.
2. Every commit gets logged to its session: hash, files, branch, worktree.
3. A session with no tasks shows **no score / needs review**.
4. Closing anything under 100% makes a task that waits on you.
5. The 1,410 split sessions get merged, and a check fails if any come back.
6. **/live/truth/**: a script, no AI, writes the real numbers daily. Today is the baseline. **That trend is how you judge us.**

## Done this turn
- **CLAUDE.md law 5:** anything that truly needs your yes becomes a waiting task, asked again at every check-in. "A question left in a report is a dropped task."
- **ai/readme.md, top line:** the session data is the source of truth.
- **The computed-value question,** with options, is written in the Session readme.
- **`public/live/` is no longer ignored by git,** and my live pages are committed.

## Waiting on you (asking again, per the new rule)
1. **Servex restart.** The item-tool fixes are waiting on it. When?
2. **Page file to 48 GB?** It's a Windows setting plus a reboot, and only you can do it.

VS Code tabs: the `UserPromptSubmit` hook (`.claude/hooks/prompt-relay.mjs`) writes every prompt the owner submits into that tab's `session.jsonl` as a `Prompt` line. It duplicates the raw transcript on purpose: small, dated and fast to search.

```sh
git grep --untracked -lEi '"type":"Prompt","text":"[^"]*footprint' -- "$S/**"
```

Voice: the owner's words are `"from":"owner (voice)"` lines. SDK agents only see the owner's words relayed by voice ("From Michael: …"). Until one `"ask"` shape exists, search all three.

## The raw transcripts (the full story)

`~/.claude/projects/C--Code-lew42-monorepo/<session id>.jsonl`: every prompt, reply, tool call and cost. That's 9,523 files and 9.5 GB, flat, with no date folders. **Filter by modified time first**, then grep only those files (timed 2026-11-06: 577 files changed in 7 days, listed in 0.6 s; the grep took 7.7 s):

```sh
P=~/.claude/projects/C--Code-lew42-monorepo
find $P -name '*.jsonl' -mtime -7 -print0 \
 | xargs -0 grep -l '"type":"user".\{0,400\}footprint'
```

`"type":"user"` lines also carry tool results, so treat hits as candidates and read the line. Search the session logs first; go to the transcripts when you need the replies, tool calls or costs, or when the logs missed it.

## The logging contract (what to aim for)

content.text:
Yes, it's a hook, and the duplication pays for itself.

## VS Code: a hook writes your prompts
`.claude/hooks/prompt-relay.mjs` runs on every prompt you submit (`UserPromptSubmit`). It writes the prompt into that tab's `session.jsonl` as a `Prompt` line. It is a copy of the raw transcript, but it's tiny, sorted into dated folders, and searches in about a second.

```sh
S=public/framework/ai/sessions
git grep -lEi \
 '"type":"Prompt","text":"[^"]*footprint' \
 -- "$S/**"
```
That pattern matches **only your prompts**.

## SDK agents never hear you directly
Your words only reach them when voice relays them ("From Michael: …"). In voice sessions your words are logged as `"from":"owner (voice)"` lines. That makes three different shapes for "the owner asked", which is why session-truth is merging them into one `"ask"` line.

## Raw transcripts: filter by date, then grep
```sh
P=~/.claude/projects/C--Code-lew42-monorepo
find $P -name '*.jsonl' -mtime -7 -print0 \
 | xargs -0 grep -l \
   '"type":"user".\{0,400\}footprint'
```
- **Size:** 9,523 files and 9.5 GB, in one flat folder named by session id, with no date folders.
- **Filtering by modified time works:** 577 files changed in the last 7 days, listed in 0.6 s.
- **Grepping just those** took 7.7 s and found "footprint" in 6 of them.
- **One catch:** `"type":"user"` lines also contain tool results, so treat hits as candidates and check the line.

## When to use which
- **Session logs first:** fast, dated, and only the important events.
- **Raw transcripts** when you need the replies, tool calls or costs, or when the logs missed something.

Both recipes are now in `ai/sessions/doc/finding.md`, committed as 42edc59eb.

# Indexing past work: how we find what was asked, done and decided

The owner asks "didn't I ask for this?" often, and the answer has to come from the files, never from memory. This page is the one place that says how to find anything we've worked on, and what has to be logged for that to work. (Moved here from `ai/sessions/doc/finding.md`, 2026-11-06.)

**Rules.**
- The session logs are the source of truth ([ai/readme.md](readme.md)).
- A search that misses or takes more than one try gets its working query added here.
- A search that can't work, because the event was never logged, adds that event to "The logging contract" and files a task to start logging it.

## 1. Search the session logs with `git grep`

Logs live in `public/framework/ai/sessions/YYYY/MM/DD/<session folder>/*.jsonl`. **The folder path is the date and the session. A line's first key is what happened.**

`rg` is **not installed** on the owner's shells. `git grep` is built in, takes regex, and skips `node_modules`. Timed 2026-11-06 over every session file: about 0.1 s for an exact key, about 2.5 s for a regex over all of `ai/`.

```sh
S=public/framework/ai/sessions
# 1. count first
git grep --untracked -c '"queued":' -- "$S/**"
# 2. too many? narrow by day
git grep --untracked -l '"queued":' -- "$S/2026/11/06/**"
# 3. words: regex anchored on a key
git grep --untracked -lEi '"title":"[^"]*tools' -- "$S/**"
```

`--untracked` goes **before** the pattern. Use `git grep -n` to get the line number, then read only that line.

## 2. The owner's own words

| Channel | Where the words are | Search |
|---|---|---|
| VS Code tab | `Prompt` lines in `session.jsonl`, written by the `UserPromptSubmit` hook (`.claude/hooks/prompt-relay.mjs`) | `'"type":"Prompt","text":"[^"]*word'` |
| Browser voice (Dictate) | `sentences:[{n,text}]` per turn, plus `sections` (the asks, citing sentence numbers) | `'"sentences":\[[^]]*word'` |
| Claude app voice | `"from":"owner (voice)"` chat lines; `"k":"prompt"` in `essence.jsonl` | `'owner (voice)[^}]*word'` |
| SDK agents | never hear the owner directly, only relays ("From Michael: …"), which are lossy | don't treat these as the owner's words |

**Planned:** one shape for every channel. The VS Code hook also writes `sentences` (one per sentence, raw), so `'"sentences":'` finds the owner's raw words everywhere. Asks are then derived from the sentences (the `sections` model), not retyped by an agent. Owner: mastermind-session-truth.

## 3. The raw transcripts (the full story)

`~/.claude/projects/C--Code-lew42-monorepo/<session id>.jsonl` holds every prompt, reply, tool call and cost. That's 9,523 files and 9.5 GB, flat, with no date folders. **Filter by modified time first**, then grep only those files. Timed 2026-11-06: 577 files changed in 7 days, listed in 0.6 s; the grep took 7.7 s.

```sh
P=~/.claude/projects/C--Code-lew42-monorepo
find $P -name '*.jsonl' -mtime -7 -print0 \
 | xargs -0 grep -l '"type":"user".\{0,400\}footprint'
```

`"type":"user"` lines also carry tool results, so treat hits as candidates. **Planned:** archive older transcripts compressed, never delete them; they're the record of every ask.

## 4. Git history: what changed, when and why

```sh
# every commit to one file (follows renames)
git log --follow --oneline -- Servex/agents/page_tools.js
# commits that ADDED or REMOVED a string
git log -S'live_root' --oneline
# commits whose diff matches a regex
git log -G'tool(\"page_' --oneline
# a string in an old version of the repo
git grep 'live_root' <commit> -- Servex/
```

Session logs only grow, so old versions of them add nothing; history is for code and docs. **Gap:** only about 1 in 10 commits names its session today. Planned: every commit logs `{"commit":…}` to its session (mastermind-session-truth).

## 5. What each event looks like

| To find | Search for | Status |
|---|---|---|
| An agent's session | `"agent":"<id>"` in `session.jsonl` | works |
| Today's VS Code tabs | `"kind":"vscode-tab"` | works |
| A task by its title | `"title":"[^"]*word` in `task.jsonl` / `session.jsonl` | works |
| A finished task | `"complete":{"outcome":` | works |
| Who started process 1234 | `"pid":1234` | planned (mastermind-resources) |
| A queued spawn | `"queued":` | planned (mastermind-resources) |
| Which session made a commit | `"commit":"abc123"` | planned (mastermind-session-truth) |
| A caught error | `"error":` | planned (mastermind-resources) |

## 6. The logging contract

One event, one line, **one fixed first key**, plus `by` and `ts`. The same event is always written the same way, whoever writes it.

```js
{ "sentences": [{ "n": 1, "text": "…" }] }
{ "queued": { "agent": "x", "commit_pct": 82 } }
{ "pid": 1234, "cmd": "…", "why": "…" }
{ "pid_exit": 1234, "code": 0 }
{ "commit": "abc123", "files": ["…"] }
{ "error": "…", "where": "file:line" }
```

## 7. What already exists (the map)

Similar things live in several places. Each one should point to the others, and some should be merged.

| What | Where | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Search past work before building | `Server/PastWork.mjs`, the `past-work` skill (`.claude/skills/past-work/`) | writes `past-work.md` per spawn; exact words only; its index (`ai/past-work-index.md`) is stale since 10-14 |
| Find sessions by tag, system, cost or day; one session's completion | `Server/session-query.mjs` ([record-spec.md](sessions/doc/data/record-spec.md), "Asking about past sessions") | completion calls `session.completion_score()` |
| One row per task, agent, card, ask | `Server/doc/ai-index.md` (AIIndex) | |
| Every task in memory, plain JS queries | `Server/doc/session-index.md` | |
| Work since 10-20, by area | [doc/built-index.md](doc/built-index.md) | hand-written, 11-01 |
| Asks vs. outcomes | [doc/asks-outcomes.md](doc/asks-outcomes.md), [doc/audits.md](doc/audits.md) | |
| How readmes work, what each role reads | [doc/readme-system.md](doc/readme-system.md), [agents.md](agents.md) | **also** `Servex/agents/roles/` (one readme per role). Two homes for agent docs: to be cross-linked, then merged into `framework/ai` |

**Readmes are the first index.** A folder's `readme.md` is short. It names everything directly inside the folder (or links a sub-doc that does) and says how to search its data. When a search was hard, the folder's readme gets the query that worked ([doc/readme-system.md](doc/readme-system.md)).

input.text:
From Michael, sharpening the pid work:
- EVERY process we start gets {"pid":…,"cmd","why","agent","started"}, and a {"pid_exit":…,"ended","code"} line when it ends. That covers Playwright browsers, worktree dev servers, the shell/bash/grep each tool call runs, and claude.exe. A pid with a start and no exit is a leak by definition. For each leak, find whether cleanup errored or an edge case was missed, and fix the cause.
- NEVER kill a Chrome process unless it is provably ours (Playwright's own command line or user-data-dir). Michael's own Chrome, VS Code and Figma are suggestions only.
- The page file is insurance, not the fix. Michael agrees the real fix is leak accounting.
- Michael wants the big "Servex is down" banner on the site turned into a subtle status indicator (e.g. in a status/dev toolbar). It should only be prominent when a voice session depends on Servex. Note it for whoever owns that UI, or do it if it's small.
The search contract for these lines is in public/framework/ai/indexing-past-work.md (it replaces sessions/doc/finding.md). Update its section-5 table when each key is live.

- Don't invent an "ask" line. Use the browser voice model that already works: each turn stores `sentences:[{n,text}]` (raw, one per sentence) plus `sections` (the asks, citing sentence numbers); see 2026/11/01/v-15bsa90/session.jsonl. Make the VS Code UserPromptSubmit hook (.claude/hooks/prompt-relay.mjs) also write `sentences`, and make the Claude-app voice log the same shape. Then '"sentences":' finds the owner's raw words on every channel, and tasks are derived from sections, not retyped by agents. SDK relays ("From Michael: …") are lossy, so the raw sentences are the record.
- Abandon old systems: remove the legacy flat sessions/<full uuid>/ route, and every doc or prompt that tells an agent its folder is there (the VS Code mastermind gave Michael that path today). One folder per session, one way to address it.
- The doc is now public/framework/ai/indexing-past-work.md (it replaces sessions/doc/finding.md). Keep its tables current as each piece lands.
- Later, not now: archive old raw transcripts in ~/.claude/projects compressed, never deleted, and post-process past sentences to find asks that were made and never done.

Servex is restarting now, so it isn't answering for the moment. In 3 minutes I'll check that it's back, that both masterminds are still running, and that the item-tool fix is live.

## finding.md wasn't lost
It was linked from CLAUDE.md, the sessions readme and the ai readme. I've now **folded it into `public/framework/ai/indexing-past-work.md`**, deleted the old file, and pointed every link at the new one. It's linked from five places:
- **CLAUDE.md**, under "Where to look"
- **ai/readme.md**: the top rule, plus its own line in "Every system"
- **the sessions readme**
- **ai/doc/readme-system.md**
- **Servex/agents/roles/readme.md**

That doc now covers:
- `git grep` recipes for the session logs
- **your own words, per channel:** VS Code `Prompt` lines, browser-voice `sentences`, app-voice chat lines
- **raw transcripts:** filter by date first, then grep
- **git history:** `git log -S`, `-G`, `--follow`
- **the logging contract**
- **a map of every index we already have:** PastWork.mjs, the past-work skill, session-query, AIIndex, SessionIndex, built-index, and asks-outcomes

## Two homes for agent docs, now cross-linked
`Servex/agents/roles/` and `framework/ai/` (agents.md, readme-system.md) now point at each other. Both are marked "to be merged into framework/ai".

## Your other points, handed off
- **mastermind-session-truth:** use the browser-voice `sentences` + `sections` shape for your words on every channel. The VS Code hook writes `sentences` too, and agents don't retype anything. Also remove the old flat `sessions/<uuid>/` route and any doc that tells agents their folder is there. Later: archive the raw transcripts, compressed and never deleted, then mine them for asks that were never done.
- **mastermind-resources:** every process gets a start line and an exit line. That covers Playwright, dev servers, the bash and grep each tool call starts, and claude.exe. A start with no exit is a leak, and it fixes the cause of each one. Chrome only gets killed if it's provably Playwright. The big "Servex down" banner becomes a subtle status indicator.
- **The voice instructions** now say a Servex restart needs no question.

**Page file:** I agree it's only insurance against crashes. The real fix is tracking every process from start to exit, which is underway.

Usage is at 19% of the week, which is 65% of pace.

{
  "ok": true,
  "truncated": false,
  "text": "# agents.md: what every agent reads first, whoever made it

This is the short base for any agent on this repo (a mastermind or a worker, Claude or another model). It points; it does not repeat. [CLAUDE.md](../../../CLAUDE.md) is the same idea written for Claude Code and stays Claude-specific; the [ai readme](readme.md) indexes the AI system and a plain agent does not need it.

## Read, in this order

1. [public/framework/readme.md](../readme.md): the module index and the framework's rules.
2. Your role's readme if you have one ([Servex/agents/roles/readme.md](../../../Servex/agents/roles/readme.md) lists them). A Servex agent already has it in its system prompt.
3. The readme of the folder you will work in, root down to leaf, then its `doc/`.
4. [handover.md](handover.md) and `git log --oneline -20`.

## The laws, in one line each (full text: [CLAUDE.md](../../../CLAUDE.md) "Laws")

- Simplest working version first; clear beats brief; most important first.
- Build what the owner asked, in the owner's words; say why if you differ.
- Keep working; never wait on the owner. Files are the only memory: if it is not committed, it did not happen.
- One of everything: use or extend what exists. Compute, don't recall: numbers come from a script.
- Name and home a new thing first; document its structure as you build it; index everything you create.
- **Readmes are the index.** Each lists everything directly inside its folder (or links a sub-doc that does). When a lookup is hard, write the search recipe into the nearest readme once you've solved it (example: [sessions, "How to find things"](sessions/readme.md#how-to-find-things)). Long form: [doc/rules.md](../doc/rules.md), "Readmes are the cheap index". (the owner, 2026-11-06)
- **Every class gets one lean core test** (`X.test.mjs` beside it): make one instance, exercise the top ~50% of what it does, assert after each call, stay well under 1 s. Add it when you build or first change a class that has none; don't over-test. How, and what earns more: [core/Test](../core/Test/readme.md).

## ⚠ One folder per session (the owner, asked many times; 2026-11-06)

A session has exactly ONE folder: `public/framework/ai/sessions/YYYY/MM/DD/<folder>/`, the day it began. The url `/framework/ai/sessions/<uuid>/` only redirects there; never create, name or write a folder `sessions/<uuid>/`. Your session's folder is printed at start ("Your session is …; its one folder is …"). In code, find it with `SessionFolders.at(store).of(id)` (its own folder) or `.record_of(id)` (where its record sits, nested for a spawned agent) ([core/Session/SessionFolders.mjs](../core/Session/SessionFolders.mjs)), never by building a path; make it with `.create(id, {first})` (or `Session.create({id, name, parent, first})`), the one creator. A check fails loudly on a flat folder: `node Server/SessionConsolidate.mjs --check`. Details: [sessions/doc/one-folder.md](sessions/doc/one-folder.md).

## Probable direction: agents in the dev server (the owner, 2026-11-06; not built)

SDK agents would run inside each project's dev server, not in Servex. That gives one item cache shared by the browser, the agents and MCP. Servex would shrink to a manager, and each project would get its own scoped MCP and `spawn_agent`. Tradeoffs, open questions and the alternative: [Servex/readme.md](../../../Servex/readme.md#probable-direction-agents-run-in-the-projects-dev-server-the-owner-2026-11-06-not-built). Until it is built, nothing changes: agents still run in Servex.

## Explaining to the owner

- **Show an API as JavaScript or pseudocode** (`page.tabs.add({name: "today"})`), not as a JSON delta, unless the owner asks what the delta looks like. Say which object the call operates on (`page`, `page.items`, a card). (the owner, 2026-11-06)

## Safety and cost (full text: [doc/agent-rules.md](doc/agent-rules.md))

- Never destructive: move aside, never delete logs or history. Never push, force or skip hooks.
- Work in a worktree, commit by exact path, smoke-test, review, then merge.
- Mind the token burn: let a script read and count, batch calls, keep sessions short. Over pace means Sonnet, fewer agents.

## Work as a task

Open a task before real work, log as you go, close it: [doc/task-buckets.md](doc/task-buckets.md). A fresh agent must be able to continue from the task folder alone. Keep a working agent rather than switching for context size alone (fresh sessions make sense around 300–500k or when a project is documented); decisions go in the module's docs as they are made ([doc/context.md](doc/context.md)).

## Where this file goes

How it reaches an agent, and why it is a system prompt and not a message: [doc/agent-base-proposal.md](doc/agent-base-proposal.md).
"

{
